prayer.text: Seven Founders of the Servite Order, pray for us.

cues.text: Seven Merchants of Florence

In 1233, seven young men of noble Florentine families — Bonfilius, Alexis, Manettus, Amadeus, Hugh, Sostene, and Buonagiunta — belonged together to a lay confraternity of laymen devoted to praising Mary, known as the Laudesi .
According to tradition, the seven were gathered in prayer on the feast of the Assumption.
Each separately experienced a vision of the Blessed Virgin urging them to leave the world and devote themselves entirely to God, without knowing the others had seen it too.
A Shared, Independent Call
Struck by the extraordinary fact that all seven had received the identical call at the same moment, the men abandoned their trades and families.
They withdrew first to La Camarzia, a house just outside Florence's walls, and later sought greater seclusion in the remote heights of Monte Senario , eleven miles north of the city.
A Second Vision and a Rule
At Monte Senario, tradition holds the seven received a further vision of Our Lady, surrounded by angels bearing instruments of Christ's Passion.
She presented them with a black habit and the Rule of St. Augustine, formally commissioning them as her Servants — the origin of the order's name, the Servants of Mary, or Servites.
Founding an Order
Only gradually did the community draw novices and formal ecclesiastical recognition.
It received papal approval in stages: papal approval from Alexander IV in 1256, and full, explicit approbation only in 1304 from Pope Benedict XI, over seventy years after the original vision.
The order spread from its Tuscan beginnings into houses across Siena, Pistoia, Arezzo, and eventually all of Europe.
Devotion to the Sorrows of Mary
Central to the spirituality the seven founders bequeathed to their order was a deep devotion to the Seven Sorrows of Mary .

This devotion involved standing at the foot of the Cross in her compassion for her Son's suffering and would, in later centuries, become one of the Servite Order's most distinctive and widely propagated contributions to the wider Church's Marian piety.
Legacy
All seven founders died at Monte Senario or in the order's other houses across the following decades, and their shared cause for canonization concluded together.
Beatified in 1717 and canonized jointly by Pope Leo XIII in 1888, they remain unusual among the Church's saints, honored not as individuals but as a single company of seven men.
Their common vision, and common vocation, founded a religious order that endures across five continents today.
